sources.title: Simone de Beauvoir
sources.note: Beauvoir's original contributions extend across existentialism, ethics and feminism. The entry challenges her treatment as merely Sartre's assistant and separates fiction, memoir and theory.

targets.A: Adds feminist philosophy and aging to broad book discovery.
targets.N: Identifies feminist and social-critical nonfiction, distinct from her novels.
targets.B: Supports original philosophical contributions across several books.
targets.P: Corrects the reduction of Beauvoir's thought to Sartre's influence.

sources.title: Hannah Arendt
sources.note: Origins of Totalitarianism, The Human Condition and Eichmann in Jerusalem had academic and public impact. They investigate different questions; the banality-of-evil formulation remains controversial.

targets.A: Adds political history, philosophy and trial reportage.
targets.N: Maps different nonfiction forms rather than treating all books as theoretical treatises.
targets.B: Distinguishes political philosophy from reportage within Arendt's corpus.
targets.P: Supports public and scholarly reception while preserving controversy.

sources.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
sources.note: Tractatus and Philosophical Investigations represent major approaches to language and philosophy. The familiar early/late split is itself disputed by scholarship emphasizing continuity or additional phases.

targets.N: Adds argumentative nonfiction with interpretive uncertainty.
targets.B: Requires separate work-level evidence for early and later approaches.
targets.P: Documents influence without assuming a simple reversal narrative.

sources.title: David Hume
sources.note: Hume's contemporary historical fame differed from later philosophical reception. The Enquiries rework Treatise topics more concisely; scholarship debates continuity and substantive change.

targets.A: Adds Enlightenment philosophy and a reception-versus-accessibility contrast.
targets.N: Distinguishes the Treatise from its later nonfiction reworkings.
targets.B: Supports comparing original and revised philosophical arguments.
targets.P: Documents experimental approach and evolving reception.

sources.title: Baruch Spinoza
sources.note: Spinoza links naturalistic metaphysics to passions, happiness and democratic politics. The entry separately treats Ethics and the Theological-Political Treatise.

targets.N: Identifies two substantive argumentative nonfiction works.
targets.B: Maps ethics and politics to distinct works.
targets.P: Supports Spinoza's original synthesis of several intellectual traditions.

sources.title: Thomas Aquinas
sources.note: Aquinas systematically reworked Aristotelian thought. His Summae are theological works with philosophical content; serious comparison should include disputed questions and parallel treatments.

targets.A: Adds medieval systematic theology and philosophy.
targets.B: Distinguishes philosophical contribution from modern genre labels.
targets.P: Documents scholastic innovation and subsequent debate.

sources.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
sources.note: Nietzsche combines psychological critique with proposed new values. The Will to Power is a posthumous notebook selection, unlike the authored Genealogy and Beyond Good and Evil.

targets.A: Adds cultural criticism with a concrete editorial-authenticity warning.
targets.N: Separates published critical books from later notebook compilation.
targets.B: Supports work-level evidence and edition-sensitive reading.
targets.P: Documents Nietzsche's philosophical projects beyond isolated slogans.

sources.title: Frantz Fanon
sources.note: Black Skin, White Masks develops anti-racist humanism; later works shift toward colonized peoples' liberation. The entry places Fanon centrally in Africana political thought.

targets.A: Adds anti-colonial social and political books.
targets.N: Distinguishes personal-racial analysis from later decolonization studies.
targets.B: Establishes philosophical content and development across Fanon's works.
targets.P: Supports Fanon's role in Africana thought and human dignity debates.

sources.limits: Interpretive introduction; debates over violence and later reception need independent criticism.
